paragraphs: It was a warm, bright day at the end of August. The meeting with the elder had been set for half-past eleven, right after late mass. Our visitors did not attend the service. They arrived just as it ended. First came an elegant open carriage drawn by two valuable horses, carrying Miüsov and a distant relative of his, a young man of twenty named Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov. The young man was getting ready to enter university. He was staying with Miüsov for now, and Miüsov kept urging him to go abroad, to the university at Zurich or Jena. The young man still hadn’t decided. He was thoughtful and absent-minded. He was good-looking, strongly built, and fairly tall. At times his gaze had a strange fixity. Like all very absent-minded people, he would sometimes stare at a person without seeing him. He was silent and rather awkward. But sometimes, when he was alone with someone, he became talkative and gushing, and would laugh at anything or nothing. His liveliness vanished as quickly as it came. He was always well dressed, even elaborately so. He already had some independent money and expected much more. He was a friend of Alyosha’s.

A long way behind Miüsov’s carriage came Fyodor Pavlovitch with his son Ivan, in an ancient, jolting but roomy hired carriage drawn by a pair of old pinkish-gray horses. Dmitri was late, though he had been told the time the evening before. The visitors left their carriage at the hotel outside the monastery grounds and walked to the monastery gates. Apart from Fyodor Pavlovitch, none of them had ever seen the monastery, and Miüsov had probably not set foot in a church for thirty years. He looked around with curiosity and an air of assumed ease. But apart from the church and the service buildings, which were ordinary enough too, he found nothing of interest inside the monastery. The last of the worshippers were coming out of the church, bareheaded and crossing themselves. Among the humbler people there were a few of higher rank, two or three ladies and a very old general. They were all staying at the hotel. Beggars at once surrounded our visitors, but none of them gave anything, except young Kalganov. He took a ten-copeck piece out of his purse and, nervous and embarrassed (God knows why!), hurriedly gave it to an old woman, saying, “Divide it equally.” None of his companions said a word about it, so he had no reason to be embarrassed. But when he saw that, he felt even more flustered.

It was strange that nobody seemed to expect them, and that they were not received with any special honor. One of them had recently donated a thousand roubles, and another was a very rich, highly cultured landowner. In a sense the whole monastery depended on him, because a court ruling in the lawsuit might at any moment hand their fishing rights over to him. Yet no one in authority came out to meet them.

Miüsov looked absent-mindedly at the tombstones around the church. He was about to say that the dead buried here must have paid a pretty penny for the right to lie in this “holy place,” but he held back. His liberal irony was quickly turning almost into anger.
“Who the devil is there to ask in this idiotic place? We must find out, because time is passing,” he said suddenly, as if talking to himself.

All at once an elderly, bald man came up, with ingratiating little eyes, wearing a full summer overcoat. Lifting his hat, he introduced himself in a honeyed lisp as Maximov, a landowner from Tula. He at once took up our visitors’ problem.
“Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, on his own. It’s four hundred paces from the monastery, past the copse.”
“I know it’s on the other side of the copse,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, “but we don’t remember the way. It’s a long time since we were last here.”
“This way, through this gate, and straight across the copse ... the copse. Come with me, won’t you? I’ll show you. I have to go.... I’m going there myself. This way, this way.”

They left by the gate and headed for the copse. Maximov was sixty, and he half ran as he went, twisting sideways to stare at each of them with an incredible, jittery curiosity. His eyes looked as if they might pop out of his head.

“You see, we’re visiting the elder on private business,” Miüsov said sternly. “That gentleman has given us an audience, so to speak. We thank you for pointing out the way, but we can’t invite you to come along.”
“Oh, I’ve been there. I’ve been already; _un chevalier parfait_!” And Maximov snapped his fingers in the air.
“Who is a _chevalier_?” asked Miüsov.
“The elder! The splendid elder, the elder! Zossima, the honor and glory of the monastery. What an elder he is!”
But his rambling was cut short by a monk who caught up with them, a very pale, worn-looking man of medium height in a monk’s cap. Fyodor Pavlovitch and Miüsov stopped.
With a deep and very courteous bow, the monk announced:
“The Father Superior asks all of you gentlemen to dine with him once you’ve finished at the hermitage. At one o’clock, not a minute later. You too,” he added, turning to Maximov.

“I’ll certainly come, without fail,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, enormously pleased at the invitation. “And believe me, we’ve all given our word to behave properly here.... And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, will you go too?”
“Yes, of course. What did I come for, if not to study all the customs here? The only thing in my way is your company....”
“Yes, Dmitri Fyodorovitch doesn’t exist yet.”
“It would be a splendid thing if he never turned up. Do you think I enjoy any of this, and with you along, too? So, we’ll come to dinner. Thank the Father Superior,” he told the monk.
“No, it’s my duty now to take you to the elder,” answered the monk.
“Then I’ll go to the Father Superior right now—right to the Father Superior,” babbled Maximov.
“The Father Superior is occupied at the moment. But do as you wish—” the monk said, hesitating.
“Impertinent old man!” Miüsov said aloud, as Maximov ran back to the monastery.
“He’s like von Sohn,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly.
“Is that the best you can come up with?... How is he like von Sohn? Have you ever even seen von Sohn?”
“I’ve seen his portrait. It’s not the features, it’s something you can’t quite name. He’s a second von Sohn. I can always tell from the physiognomy.”

“Ah, I’m sure you’re an expert on that. But listen, Fyodor Pavlovitch. You said yourself a minute ago that we’d given our word to behave. Remember that. Keep a grip on yourself, I’m advising you. If you start playing the fool, I won’t be seen with you here.... You see the kind of man he is”—he turned to the monk—“I’m afraid to go among decent people with him.” A faint smile, with a touch of slyness in it, crossed the pale, bloodless lips of the monk. He said nothing in reply, obviously staying quiet out of a sense of his own dignity. Miüsov frowned harder than ever.
“Oh, devil take them all! A show put on for the outside, built up over centuries, and nothing but charlatanism and nonsense underneath,” flashed through Miüsov’s mind.
“There’s the hermitage. We’re here,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “The gates are closed.”
And he crossed himself again and again before the saints painted above the gates and on either side of them.

“When in Rome, do as the Romans do. In this hermitage there are twenty-five saints working out their salvation. They gaze at each other and eat cabbage. And not a single woman passes through this gate. That’s the remarkable thing. And it’s really true. But I did hear that the elder receives ladies,” he said suddenly to the monk.

“There are peasant women here right now too, lying in the portico, waiting. For ladies of higher rank, two rooms have been built beside the portico, but outside the grounds—you can see the windows—and the elder goes out to them through an inner passage when he is well enough. They always stay outside the grounds. A lady from Harkov, Madame Hohlakov, is waiting there now with her sick daughter. He has probably promised to come out to her, though he has been so weak lately that he has barely shown himself even to the common people.”

“So there are loopholes after all, to slip out of the hermitage to the ladies. Don’t think, holy father, that I mean any harm. But do you know, on Athos not only are visits from women forbidden, but no creature of the female sex is allowed—no hens, no turkey-hens, no cows.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, I warn you, I’ll go back and leave you here. They’ll throw you out as soon as I’m gone.”
“But I’m not getting in your way, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Look,” he cried suddenly, stepping inside the grounds, “what a valley of roses they live in!”

Though there were no roses now, there were masses of rare and beautiful autumn flowers growing wherever there was room for them, plainly tended by a skillful hand. There were flower-beds around the church and between the tombs. The one-story wooden house where the elder lived was also surrounded by flowers.
“And was it like this under the last elder, Varsonofy? He had no taste for such refinement. They say he’d leap up and thrash even ladies with a stick,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, going up the steps.

“The elder Varsonofy did sometimes seem rather strange, but a great deal of what’s told about him is foolishness. He never beat anyone,” answered the monk. “Now, gentlemen, if you’ll wait a minute, I’ll announce you.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the last time, remember your promise, do you hear? Behave properly or I’ll make you pay for it!” Miüsov had time to mutter once more.

“I can’t think why you’re so worked up,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said sarcastically. “Are you uneasy about your sins? They say he can tell from a person’s eyes what he’s come about. And how much you think of their opinion, you, a Parisian, and so advanced! I’m surprised at you.”
Miüsov had no time to answer the jibe. They were called in. He went in feeling rather irritated.
“Now, I know myself. I’m annoyed, I’ll lose my temper and start quarreling—and lower myself and my ideas,” he thought.
